html:
The Battle of Inchon was a landing from the sea on 15 September 1950 at the port of Incheon, on the west coast of Korea near Seoul. United Nations forces under the American general Douglas MacArthur landed far behind the North Korean army and turned the Korean War around.

North Korea had invaded the South in June 1950 and pushed the South Korean and American forces into a small corner around Busan. MacArthur planned to strike more than 200 km behind the front. Incheon was a hard place to land: the tide rose and fell about 9 metres and left wide mud flats, the channel was narrow, and the city had sea walls, not beaches. But the port was lightly held. Marines took the island guarding the harbour on the morning tide and the city on the evening one. Seoul was retaken within two weeks. The troops at Busan broke out, and the North Korean army, cut off from its supplies, fell apart.

UN forces then crossed the 38th parallel and drove north toward China's border. China entered the war in October and pushed them back. The fighting ended in 1953 near where it began.
